clue.text: Soften tobacco, say, doubly loudly – for puffer? (4-4)

indicators.note: 'doubly' asks for the same piece over again, so whatever the first half hands you gets written out twice.
'loudly' is about saying a word rather than spelling it, so what goes in the grid is what the ear hears.

blocks.note: a plug of tobacco is softened between the teeth, and the word for doing that, said out loud, is written this way in the nursery
the same noise is called for a second time

explanation.surface: Tobacco worked soft and a shout repeated twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffer' looks like a fish or an inhaler and is the nursery word for a steam engine. A chew is the wad of tobacco you soften in your cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: A puffer is a steam locomotive, and the nursery name for one imitates the noise it makes going along.

blocks.note: a true Cockney is born within the sound of Bow Bells, the church bells of Bow in London's East End
the eighteenth-century Venetian's name is the byword for a great seducer

explanation.surface: An East End ladies' man, held up as something to take your breath away.
explanation.walkthrough: The break in the wordplay is not the break in the answer: the two pieces divide one letter earlier than the two words that go in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl someone over is to knock them flat, and the figurative sense — leave them astonished — is the one in everyday use.

indicators.note: 'barely' is stripped bare, and a word stripped bare gives up the letters standing on its outside.
the '-bound' half is the instruction: anyone bound to a house cannot get out of it, so the house closes round what follows.

blocks.note: the House of York, the royal house of the white rose in the Wars of the Roses
the outer S and K are stripped off, leaving the two letters in the middle

explanation.surface: A sickly figure who can barely get out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' is the royal House of York rather than a home, so the invalid stuck indoors is a picture the surface paints and the wordplay never uses.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: Yorick was the king's jester in Hamlet, remembered as the skull Hamlet holds in the graveyard.

clue.text: Rule with old king in new seat (7)

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece within another instead of alongside it, so the king lands in the middle rather than at the end.
'new' means made afresh, and letters made afresh come out in an order the clue has not printed.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder
Tutankhamun, the boy pharaoh, is the old king crosswords keep on the shelf

explanation.surface: A coronation: an old monarch installed on a newly made throne.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the coronation picture is doing letter work, and Tut is the standard crossword king — three letters, permanently available, no other pharaoh so short.
explanation.definitionFit: A statute is a law as written down by a legislature, which is the formal sense of a rule imposed rather than a rule of thumb.

clue.text: A taboo embraced by goddess in aria (8)

indicators.note: 'embraced by' is a hug: whatever does the embracing opens its arms and takes the other piece inside.

blocks.note: Hera, queen of the Greek gods and wife of Zeus
a taboo is a ban, and the clue's own A comes along with it

explanation.surface: A goddess folding something forbidden into her arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's opening 'A' belongs to the wordplay rather than to the grammar, which is the hardest thing to see here. Hera is the four-letter goddess setters reach for first.
explanation.definitionFit: A habanera is a Cuban dance song, and the famous one is Carmen's, so 'aria' names it by its best-known example.

blocks.note: a brand is the design a company stamps on what it sells
the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
to shed something is to drop it, the way a tree sheds leaves

explanation.surface: A design its creator abandoned went on to thrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourished' is the waving sense, not the thriving one the surface offers, and 'dropped' is a synonym at work rather than the fate of the design.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandished and flourished are the same act in the past tense: a sword or a document waved about for show.

definitions.note: 'Wood' is a mass noun where the answer is plural: the second definition names the answer by the stuff it is cut from, sawn lengths of it.

blocks.note: the British insult for the very dim, as in 'thick as two short ones'
sawn timber, the boards a mill turns a trunk into

explanation.surface: Idiots blundering about in a wood.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang makes a plank a dolt — 'thick as two short planks' is the phrase behind it — so both halves of the clue are talking about the same timber.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: in British usage a plank is a blockhead, and planks are also the sawn boards cut out of a tree.

blocks.note: 'shoo' is what you say to drive a cat or a pigeon away
a tout pitches tickets to passers-by outside the ground

explanation.surface: A player walking off the pitch just as the decider begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave pitch' looks like one football instruction and is two words clued separately — an order to be off, and the patter of a man selling tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: A shootout is the climactic gunfight of a western, and a penalty shootout is the battle that finally settles a drawn tie.

indicators.note: 'set' is the printer's word for type arranged on a page, and type arranged again comes out in a different order.

blocks.note: thirteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Somebody asking when the nastiest snares get laid.
explanation.walkthrough: Every 10 in this grid is a fool, and this is the day they own — the puzzle was published on it. 'Filthier traps' reads as the snares of the surface and is thirteen letters waiting to be moved.
explanation.definitionFit: 'When?' is answered by a date, and this is the date on which the tricks the surface describes are traditionally sprung.

blocks.note: the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream who is given an ass's head, offered as one instance rather than a synonym
'sweet' is the British name for the dessert course, and this one is fruit crushed into whipped cream

explanation.surface: A bottom described, oddly enough, as something sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: Seven other clues in this grid point back at this one, because the answer is the puzzle's theme. A gooseberry fool is the pudding; Bottom is only one of Shakespeare's many candidates.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom, the ass-headed weaver, is one instance of the word; the other sense is the pudding of fruit whipped into cream.

clue.text: Moderation ultimately cutting it, wet acquiring skills (2,8)

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means at the very end, and the end of the word beside it is where the single letter comes from.
someone cutting in pushes into the middle of something already under way, so the letter lands inside rather than after.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, taken as it stands, and about to be split open
the closing letter of moderation
when it is wet outside, it is raining

explanation.surface: Restraint at last proving good enough, while a soggy sort picks up new skills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting it' reads as the idiom for being good enough, and the two words are not even in the same piece of the wordplay: one is an instruction, the other is material.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in training is acquiring skills — the phrase covers athletes and apprentices alike, both still mid-process rather than finished.

clue.text: Cane has whipped hard in routine (6)

indicators.note: to whip something, in British slang, is to pinch it, and what the cane pinches it keeps inside itself.

blocks.note: a cane is a stick
H = hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.surface: A cane coming down hard, apparently as part of somebody's regular practice.
explanation.walkthrough: Shtick is Yiddish for a piece or slice, and a comic's shtick is the bit of business they do every time out. 'Whipped' is the pickpocket's sense here, not the beating the surface shows.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer's shtick is the routine they are known for — the same gag or turn wheeled out at every appearance.

clue.text: The satanic works, atheist can too then! (2,4,4)

indicators.note: 'works' claims the phrase functions as raw material: put to work, its letters take up new positions.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder
these three words hold the very same ten letters over again, which is the setter's joke rather than extra material

explanation.surface: A claim that satanic writings work, and that an atheist could manage as much.
explanation.walkthrough: Both phrases carry the same ten letters: 'the satanic' and 'atheist can' each rearrange into IN THAT CASE, and the exclamation mark is the setter enjoying the coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Then' in the sense of 'if so': 'then I'll walk' and 'in that case I'll walk' are the same sentence.

indicators.note: 'has taken in' is what a household does with a lodger: the next piece is given a room inside.

blocks.note: a cod is a hoax, and cod as an adjective means fake
a famous name is a star

explanation.surface: A hoax that has swallowed a celebrity whole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cod' for a hoax survives in codswallop and cod Latin. A costard is also a big old English apple, which is where the character got his name.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: Costard is the rustic clown of Love's Labour's Lost, the comic simpleton the play sends about with letters.

clue.text: Record for example in brief, bar lifted? (8)

indicators.note: 'in' is a placement word: what comes before it is dropped inside what comes after.
'lifted' is the shoplifter's sense — the bar is pinched from the word and carried off.

blocks.note: in British slang your brief is your barrister, the lawyer arguing your case, and BAR is lifted off the front of him
the everyday two-letter shorthand for 'for example'

explanation.surface: Something noted down in a lawyer's summary once the bar has been raised.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a brief is a barrister, so the bar comes off the man and not off the document. Reading 'lifted' as a raising, which a down clue would license, is the false trail: it means stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: A register is a record kept in a book — the roll a school calls or a church writes marriages into.

clue.text: Rat traps however ending in pipe where current flows (7)

indicators.note: a trap holds on to whatever walks into it, so the word before it shuts around the next piece.
'ending in' points at the final letter of the word that follows it.

blocks.note: a rat is a cad, an untrustworthy sort
tho' is the poetic short form of though
the last letter of pipe

explanation.surface: Rat traps laid at the end of a pipe with water running through it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is plumbing and vermin and the answer is electrical. Tho' is the sort of poetic contraction setters keep on hand whenever three awkward letters are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathode is an electrode: the terminal in a valve, tube or cell that the current passes through.

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them doggedly about
a berry is the small soft fruit on a bush

explanation.surface: A plant stalk with its fruit still attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalk' is the verb here while the surface keeps it botanical alongside the fruit. Dogberry's mangled words — 'Comparisons are odorous' — are what Shakespeare built the character out of.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: Dogberry is the blundering constable of Much Ado About Nothing, the play's self-important idiot.

blocks.note: the verb sense: to leave somebody thwarted and out of options, which is what a trickster does to a mark
the one played on green baize with fifteen reds, six colours and a rest

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe reads as a possessive and is standing in for 'is', with a definition either side of it. The verb comes from the table game: leave your opponent no shot and you have snookered them.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: to snooker someone is to outwit them into a hopeless position, and snooker is also the baize game itself.

clue.text: Aerosol device possibly empty, gas having run out (5-3)

indicators.note: 'empty' hollows a word out: the middle goes and only the letters standing at each end are left.
'out' here is out of order, so the letters gathered up do not stay in the sequence the clue lists them in.

blocks.note: 'possibly' with its insides gone leaves the first and last letters
three letters of fodder, taken as they stand
three more letters of fodder, again straight off the page

explanation.surface: An aerosol can that may be finished, its propellant all used up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having run out' reads as one phrase about an empty canister and is doing two jobs: the first word is material and the second is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A spray gun is the hand tool that atomises paint or pesticide into an aerosol, so the definition names it by what it produces.

clue.text: Page and covers – those to check? (6)

blocks.note: p. is the standard short form of page
a roof covers a building, and the verb is doing the work here

explanation.surface: A page and its covers, waiting for somebody to look them over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' looks like the boards of a book, keeping company with the page in the surface. Proofs are the trial pages a printer sends out so that errors get caught before the run.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofs are the trial copies read for mistakes before printing, so 'those to check' names them by the only job they exist for.

clue.text: One of seven bands that’s popular enjoy love (6)

blocks.note: in = popular, as in what is in this season
to dig something is to like it, in the slang of the sixties
in tennis love is a score of nothing, written as a zero

explanation.surface: A well-liked band, one of seven, basking in adoration.
explanation.walkthrough: The bands are the rainbow's rather than music's: Newton named seven colours so that the spectrum would match the notes of a scale, which is how a narrow blue-violet got a place of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is one of the seven colour bands Newton listed in the rainbow, sitting between blue and violet.

clue.text: Wrath appealing? Not quite for pacifist (6)

definitions.note: 'Pacifist' is a noun and the answer an adjective; the setter is using it the way we say 'pacifist sympathies', with the noun doing an adjective's work.

indicators.note: 'Not quite' stops the word just short of its full length, so the final letter never gets written down.

blocks.note: ire is wrath
NICE means appealing, and it is cut short of its last letter

explanation.surface: Wondering whether anger has its attractions, and deciding not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: Irenic comes from Eirene, the Greek goddess of peace, and describes anything meant to make peace. The question mark after 'appealing' warns that the synonym is about to be docked.
explanation.definitionFit: Irenic means aiming at peace, which is the outlook a pacifist holds — the adjective to their noun.

blocks.note: a touch of something is a small bit of it
a stone is the hard thing you stub a toe on

explanation.surface: Somebody biting down on something hard.
explanation.walkthrough: A touchstone proper is the dark stone jewellers rub gold against to judge its quality, which is where the everyday sense of a standard to measure things by comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: Touchstone is the jester who follows Rosalind and Celia into the Forest of Arden in As You Like It.

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, and 'off' is what takes it away.

blocks.note: the five-letter word for the shoreline, with its opening C taken off

explanation.surface: Somebody stripped to the waist on the beach, drying off.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is the kiln with the white cowl on its roof that dries hops for brewing, a familiar shape in the Kent countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast is a hop-drying kiln, so 'drier' names it by the single job the building was put up to do.

indicators.note: 'Interminable' means without end, so the word it describes gives up the letter it ends on.

blocks.note: the six-letter verb for what rot does to fruit, docked of the letter it ends on

explanation.surface: Endless nonsense, served up to an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rot' is the British word for nonsense in the surface and a verb in the wordplay. Feste is the jester who sings Twelfth Night out with the wind and the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 is FOOL: Feste is the licensed jester of Twelfth Night, employed at Olivia's house to be witty for a living.

clue.text: Agent exhausted having killed leader and rescued girl (8)

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and killing it takes that letter off the front.
anyone rescued is taken in and sheltered, so the girl ends up housed inside the other word.

blocks.note: WEARY is exhausted, and its leading W is killed off
a miss is a girl — the form of address for an unmarried woman

explanation.surface: An exhausted spy who has killed the boss and saved a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The thriller in the surface does its killing to a letter: 'leader' is the first character of a word. An emissary carries a message rather than a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is somebody sent on a mission on another's behalf — an agent in the diplomatic sense rather than the spying one.
